title: The First States
subtitle: Egypt and Mesopotamia, 3100 BC to 539 BC

steps.title: Narmer and the two lands
steps.text: Around 3100 BC a king named Narmer ruled the Nile valley. Many scholars consider him the unifier of Upper and Lower Egypt and the founder of its First Dynasty. A carved palette found at Hierakonpolis shows him in the crown of the south on one side and the crown of the north on the other, though whether it records a real conquest is still debated.

steps.title: Uruk, the first great city
steps.text: In southern Mesopotamia, Uruk had grown into the largest city of its time. Around 3100 BC it may have held up to 50,000 people. Thousands of clay tablets from its Eanna precinct include the earliest known examples of writing. Some name a man called Kushim, apparently a keeper of barley accounts, one of the first people whose name we can read.

steps.title: The Great Pyramid
steps.text: Around 2600 BC the pharaoh Khufu of the Fourth Dynasty had his tomb built at Giza. The Great Pyramid took about 26 years and an estimated 2.3 million blocks, some 6 million tonnes of stone, and rose 146.6 metres. It stayed the tallest structure made by human hands for more than 3,700 years.

steps.title: Sargon of Akkad
steps.text: Sargon of Akkad, who reigned from about 2334 BC, defeated Lugal-zage-si of Uruk and took the cities of Sumer. His inscriptions claim rule from the Lower Sea, the Persian Gulf, to the Upper Sea, the Mediterranean. He is often called the first ruler of an empire, though historians debate the label. His grandson Naram-Sin, shown on this stele, later claimed the status of a god.

steps.title: The ziggurat of Ur
steps.text: In the 21st century BC King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur raised a great stepped temple platform to the moon god Nanna, patron of his city. King Shulgi finished it. The base measures about 64 by 45 metres. Some fifteen centuries later the Babylonian king Nabonidus restored it, and its lowest stage was partly rebuilt in the 1980s.

steps.title: Hammurabi's laws
steps.text: Hammurabi ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BC. Near the end of his reign he had his laws, 282 in the modern numbering, carved in Akkadian cuneiform on a basalt stele 2.25 metres tall. About 600 years later it was carried off as plunder to Susa, in what is now Iran, where it was found in 1901. It now stands in the Louvre.

steps.title: Thutmose III at Megiddo
steps.text: In 1457 BC, by the commonly cited date, Thutmose III marched from the border fortress of Tjaru to Gaza in ten days, then north toward Megiddo, where a Canaanite coalition led by the king of Kadesh was waiting. He took the risky central pass, won the battle, and besieged the city for seven months. It is the first battle recorded in relatively reliable detail.

steps.title: Chariots at Kadesh
steps.text: In May 1274 BC Ramesses II led his army from Pi-Ramesses along the coast road past Gaza to Kadesh on the Orontes, near the present border of Lebanon and Syria. The Hittite king Muwatalli II was waiting. With perhaps 5,000 to 6,000 chariots on the field, it is believed to be the largest chariot battle ever fought. Both sides claimed victory; historians call it a stalemate.

steps.title: A treaty between great kings
steps.text: Around 1259 BC Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III made peace. Their agreement is the oldest known surviving peace treaty, and the only one from the ancient Near East for which both parties' versions survive: hieroglyphs on temple walls at Thebes, cuneiform tablets from the Hittite capital Hattusa. A copy is displayed at the United Nations headquarters.

steps.title: Assyria takes Memphis
steps.text: Assyria, a kingdom of the upper Tigris, now reached for the Nile. After a first invasion failed in 673 BC, King Esarhaddon came back in 671 BC with a larger army, passed through Harran, crossed Sinai with the help of its tribes, and took Memphis from Taharqa, the Kushite pharaoh. Taharqa escaped south, and in 663 BC Assyrian troops sacked Thebes.

steps.title: The fall of Nineveh
steps.text: In 612 BC a Median army under Cyaxares and a Babylonian army under Nabopolassar besieged Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, for about three months. The city was plundered and burned, and King Sin-shar-ishkun died in the siege. Within three years the Assyrian empire was gone, and Babylon was the leading city of Mesopotamia for the first time in over a thousand years.

steps.title: Cyrus enters Babylon
steps.text: In autumn 539 BC Cyrus of Persia defeated the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris. Sippar fell without a fight on 6 October, and Persian troops entered Babylon on 12 October. The Cyrus Cylinder says the city was taken without battle; Greek writers describe a siege. Nabonidus, the last Babylonian king, surrendered, and Cyrus's son Cambyses later conquered Egypt.
